_comment: Hindu expansion part 1: Rigveda hymn-myths (creation, combat, death). All passages are paraphrases of public-domain translations, each carrying a note.

title.en: The Purusha Sukta: Creation from the Sacrificed Man
title.zh: 原人歌：以犧牲之軀創世

region.zh: 旁遮普平原，梨俱吠陀核心區（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10 (late mandala), c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 90 (Purusha Sukta)

summary.en: A thousand-headed cosmic Man, Purusha, is sacrificed by the gods themselves; his body is cut up and becomes the world - sky from his head, earth from his feet, sun from his eye, moon from his mind - while the four castes spring from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet. The hymn fuses cosmogony with ritual: the world exists because it was once offered.
summary.zh: 千首千眼的宇宙巨人普魯沙為諸神所祭；其身軀被分割而化為世界——頭化天穹、足化大地、眼化太陽、心化月亮；四大種姓則出自其口、臂、腿、足。此頌將創世與祭祀合一：世界之存在，正因其曾為祭品。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: the Purusha Sukta is recited in Vedic ritual and its caste verses are politically contested in modern India. Classified 'myth' (hymn-myth rather than liturgical prescription); the contested readings are recorded in the variants and sensitivity guidance.

passages.text: Purusha has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet; he covers the earth on every side and extends ten fingers' breadth beyond it. All that is, all that has been and all that shall be, is this Man; he has become immortality and whatever the gods feed upon. Three-quarters of him rose above creation; one-quarter was spread through this world of living things, and from it he pervaded everything that eats and everything that does not eat.

When the gods spread out the sacrifice, they made of Purusha the victim: spring was the melted butter of the offering, summer the fuel, autumn the oblation. They bound the Man born of old upon the sacrificial grass and sacrificed him with the sacrifice itself; the celestial beings, the seers of old, and the offerings were made one - thus did the gods sacrifice to the sacrifice.

From that all-encompassing sacrifice the curds and butter were gathered, the victim's parts prepared; the sky came from his head, the atmosphere from his navel, the earth from his feet, the directions of space from his ear. From his mind the moon was born, from his eye the sun, from his mouth Indra and Agni, from his breath the wind; the ridges of the mountains came from him, the seas and streams were made from him.

When they divided the Man, into how many parts did they divide him? His mouth became the Brahmin, his arms the Kshatriya, his thighs the Vaishya, and from his feet the Shudra was born. The sacred word was born from the same sacrifice - the verses, the chants and the ritual formulae - together with the horse, the cow, the goat and the sheep, each from a different portion of the victim; the gods raised him up and made him the oblation.

texts.canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda, 2nd ed., Benares, 1896 (public domain); critical: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton, The Rigveda, 3 vols., Oxford University Press, 2014

narrative.en:
The Purusha Sukta is the Rigveda's most concentrated cosmogony and its most debated poem: fifteen verses in an archaic metre, placed at the head of Book 10's creation cluster. It answers the question 'how was the world made?' with a single image - a cosmic human body, offered up and divided.

The hymn opens with the Man himself. Purusha has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet; he envelops the earth and reaches ten fingers' breadth beyond it. He is not one being among others: whatever has been and whatever will be is this Man, and he is himself immortality and the food of the gods. Three-quarters of him rise above creation into the timeless; one-quarter is spread through the world of living things, and from that quarter everything that eats and everything that does not eat is pervaded.

Then comes the act. The gods - 'the celestial beings' and 'those who were seers of old' - bind Purusha, born before time, upon the sacrificial grass, and sacrifice him with the sacrifice itself. Spring supplies the melted butter, summer the fuel, autumn the offering: the ritual calendar is projected back onto the origin of the world, so that every later sacrifice re-enacts the first one. The gods 'sacrificed with the sacrifice to the sacrifice'; from the all-encompassing offering the curds and butter are gathered, and the world's body is distributed.

The dismemberment is the geography. From Purusha's mind comes the moon, from his eye the sun, from his mouth Indra and Agni, from his breath the wind. His head becomes the sky, his navel the atmosphere, his feet the earth, his ear the directions of space; the mountains are his ridges, the sea and the streams his generated waters. Light itself is part of the spent body.

Finally the social order. When they divided the Man, his mouth became the Brahmin, his arms the Kshatriya, his thighs the Vaishya, his feet the Shudra: the four classes of Vedic society are mapped onto the sacrificed body, hierarchy written into creation. The sacred word is born from the same sacrifice - the verses, the chants, the ritual formulae - together with the sacrificial animals, the horse, the cow, the goat, the sheep, each from a different portion of the victim. The gods raise Purusha up and make him the oblation.

Function: the hymn makes sacrifice the engine of the cosmos - the world is not created but offered, and ritual is therefore not man-made devotion but participation in a cosmic event. It grounds the varna system in a creation narrative and gave later thought its model of macrocosm and microcosm: the body and the universe are the same thing at two scales. In later strata, Purusha becomes the Self of the Upanishads (the second bird on the same tree in the Mundaka), and Purusha-Narayana the couch of Vishnu; this late hymn reshaped the whole tradition around itself.

The verses assigning caste have made the hymn politically contested in modern India: Dalit and reformist readings treat the caste verses as a late insertion (linguistic arguments support a late date and possible interpolation), while orthodox commentary reads them as cosmological rather than legislative. The record keeps the hymn whole and records the dispute in its variants.
narrative.zh: 原人歌為梨俱吠陀最集中的創世頌：十五節詩，以一幅圖像回答『世界如何造成』——宇宙之軀被獻祭而分割。普魯沙千首千眼千足，籠蓋大地而超出十指之寬；萬有之過去未來皆此巨人，彼即不死與諸神之食。其四分之三超出造化，四分之一遍於眾生。諸神以祭祀束縛這位太古所生之巨人，以祭祀祭之：春為酥油、夏為薪柴、秋為祭品。祭祀之後，身軀化為世界——心化月亮、眼化太陽、口生因陀羅與阿耆尼、息生風神；首化天穹、臍化空界、足化大地、耳化方位；山是其稜脊，海流由其所生。分割之際，社會秩序亦定：口生婆羅門、臂生剎帝利、腿生吠舍、足生首陀羅；頌詩、歌詠、祭祀口訣皆自同一祭中誕生，馬牛羊亦各出其身之一部。功能：以祭祀為宇宙引擎——世界非被造而是被獻，儀式遂非人為虔敬而為宇宙事件之重演；種姓制度被寫入創世敘事；宏微宇宙相即之模型由此奠定。後世層中，普魯沙化為奧義書之自我（蒙達卡奧義書同樹之雙鳥），普魯沙-那羅延化為毘濕奴之臥榻；此晚期頌歌重塑了整個傳統。種姓諸節在現代印度政治上極具爭議：賤民與改革派讀法視其為晚出插文（語文學論據支持晚期與可能之插入），正統注釋則讀為宇宙論而非立法。本錄保留全頌並於變體欄記錄爭議。

functions: Charter of Vedic sacrifice: every ritual re-enacts the primordial offering of Purusha
Mythic grounding of the four varnas and of macrocosm-microcosm correspondence
Bridge text between Vedic ritualism and Upanishadic interiority (Purusha as Self)
Recited in Agnihotra and major sacrificial rites to this day

variants.name: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad reworking (the Self divides itself)
variants.text_tradition: Brihadaranyaka 1.4, Kuru-Panchala prose, c. 8th-6th c. BCE
variants.summary: Replaces the ritual dismemberment with a Self that alone existed, feared, desired a second and divided itself - the sacrificed body becomes an internalizing meditation on the Self.

variants.name: Narayana-Purusha of the Mahabharata (Shanti Parva)
variants.summary: Epic theology identifies Purusha with Narayana-Vishnu as the universal soul from whose body the worlds proceed; the sacrifice frame softens into avatara doctrine.

variants.name: Mundaka Upanishad's two birds on one tree
variants.summary: Purusha splits into two birds - one eating the tree's sweet fruit (the engaged self), one watching without eating (the witnessing Self) - converting the hymn's cosmology into soteriology.

variants.name: Modern contested readings of the caste verses
variants.summary: Critical philology (e.g. Jamison-Brereton 2014) treats the varna verses as a likely late insertion; Ambedkarite and reform readings reject the hymn's caste grounding, while orthodox commentators read them as cosmological description, not legislation.

Quote only public-domain or critical translations; attribute mandala and hymn; present the interpolation question and the varna dispute in variants rather than asserting either as settled.

title.en: The Hiranyagarbha Hymn: Golden Womb of the Worlds

region.zh: 俱盧之野平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10 (late mandala), c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 121 (Hiranyagarbha Sukta)

summary.en: In the beginning rose the Golden Womb - Hiranyagarbha - born as the one lord of all that is; before heaven and earth were, he held within himself the gods and the worlds. Each verse ends with the refrain 'what deity shall we worship with the oblation?', and the final verse dares to doubt whether even the highest being knows - the Vedic skeptic's creation hymn that later becomes Brahma's cosmic egg.
summary.zh: 太初升起金胎——希任耶加爾波——為萬有唯一之主；天地未分，彼已內含諸神與世界。每節末句重唱『吾人以祭品當敬奉何神？』，末節更敢疑至高者是否自知——此吠陀懷疑論之創世頌，後世演化為梵天之宇宙金卵。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: recited in worship and meditated upon in Vedanta. Classified 'myth' (hymn-myth).

passages.text: In the beginning rose Hiranyagarbha, the Golden Womb, born as the only lord of all created beings. He fixed and held up this earth and heaven. Before heaven and earth had come to be, before the waters moved, that One drew breath, unborn, sustaining all things; whatever breathes and shuts its eyes looked to him alone.

The refrain runs through every verse: what deity shall we adore with the offering? The One by whose command the worlds rose, he in whom the gods found their own seats; he who holds the snow-clad mountains and the sea, the waters that encircle all; he whose are heaven and earth, the sun and the firmament - the one God above the gods.

The closing verse turns the hymn on itself: may he not harm us, he who is the procreator of the earth, who established the bright regions of heaven, the golden embryo within the waters that possessed them all - and then, with almost deliberate ambiguity, the poet asks: he who was truly the begetter, the guardian of the gods - whether he himself knows it or not - if he does not know, who among us can know?

texts.canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda, 2nd ed., Benares, 1896 (public domain); critical: Jamison & Brereton, The Rigveda, Oxford, 2014

narrative.en:
The Hiranyagarbha Sukta (Rigveda 10.121) is the second great creation hymn of Book 10, and the most theological of the Vedic hymns: a chant of ten verses, each ending with the same questioning refrain, addressed to an unnamed supreme origin.

The image: in the beginning there rose from the waters a golden embryo - a cosmic egg, golden like the sun - and it was born as the one lord of all that exists. Before the earth and heaven were made, before even the waters had spread, that One breathed, unborn, sustaining everything that breathes and shuts its eyes. From the Golden Womb the world is not so much manufactured as hatched: the One 'fixed and held up this earth and heaven', gave the gift of breath, of life, of the gods' own thrones. The mountains with their snowy peaks are his; the sea and the encircling waters are his; heaven and earth and the sun's path are his dominion.

The refrain is the hymn's signature: 'what deity shall we worship with the oblation?' - 'he, they say, is that one'. The insistence on the question rather than a name gives the hymn a monotheizing and also a deferring quality: later traditions resolve the ambiguity by naming the One - Prajapati in the Brahmanas, Brahma in the Puranas - but the Vedic poet keeps the divinity unnamed and the worship provisional.

The last verse is the sharpest: the poet prays that the golden one, procreator of the earth, establisher of the bright heavens, may not harm us - and then steps back: he who was the true begetter, the guardian of the gods, whether he himself knows it or not - 'if he does not know, who among us can know?' This is the same skeptical breath that animates the Nasadiya Sukta's closing lines ('perhaps even the highest overseer knows not'). Vedic cosmogony refuses final certainty: creation is affirmed, the creator is doubted.

Function and afterlife: the hymn supplied the tradition with its standing image for cosmic origin - hiranyagarbha, the golden egg - which the Brahmanas elaborate (the waters lay as an egg, heat matured it, Brahma broke through), which the Puranas turn into the immense Brahma-anda surrounding all worlds (see the Vishnu Purana egg record), and which Vedanta takes as a meditation-object. In ritual, 'hiranyagarbha' is also the name of an enormous royal gold-donation sacrifice: a king ceremonially reborn from a golden womb, claiming cosmic kingship by enacting the origin - the myth migrating from cosmology into consecration.
narrative.zh: 金胎頌（梨俱吠陀 10.121）為第十卷第二大創世頌，最具神學性：十節頌歌，每節同以一句疑問重唱作結，向一位未名的至上本源祈唱。意象為：太初自水中升起一金色胎卵——宇宙之卵，金如太陽——彼生而為萬有唯一之主。天地未立、諸水未布之前，此一者已呼吸，未生而養育一切凡呼吸閉目者。世界非被造而是被孵育：『彼奠定、托舉此天與地』，賜予氣息、生命與諸神之座。雪山屬彼，海與環繞之水屬彼，天與地與日行之軌屬其王權。重唱『吾人以祭品當敬奉何神？』——『彼，人言即是』——堅持以問句而非名號，使頌歌帶有獨神化而亦延宕的色彩：後世釋之為生主（梵書）、梵天（往世書），而吠陀詩人始終不名其名。末節最銳利：詩人祈求金胎者勿加害，繼而退問——彼為真正的生者、諸神之守護者，縱彼自身亦未必自知——『彼若不知，吾等誰能知？』此與無有歌結尾之懷疑同調：吠陀創世觀拒絕最終確定性。功能與後續：此頌供給傳統以『金胎』之標準宇宙起源意象——梵書演之、往世書化為梵天之巨卵、吠檀多以之為冥想對象；儀式上『金胎』亦為巨額獻金之王祭：王者自金卵中儀式性重生，以身行創世而宣稱宇宙王權。

functions: Standing Vedic image of cosmic origin (golden embryo/egg) for Brahmana, Purana and Vedanta
Theology of an unnamed supreme lord - prayer without a fixed name
Charter of the hiranyagarbha royal sacrifice (king reborn from a golden womb)
Model of reverent skepticism about final knowledge of origins

variants.name: Shatapatha Brahmana's egg-cosmogony
variants.summary: The waters lay as a cosmic egg; heat (tapas) matured it for a year; Brahma (Prajapati) broke through and created - the hymn's golden womb given narrative procedure and ritual timing.

variants.name: Vishnu Purana's Brahma-anda
variants.text_tradition: Purana corpus, Wilson translation 1840, Book 1, chs. 1-2
variants.summary: The golden egg becomes the immense cosmic egg within which Vishnu sleeps and Brahma creates at each kalpa; the Vedic image is absorbed into Puranic cosmology.

variants.name: Nasadiya Sukta's skeptical parallel
variants.summary: A companion hymn that pushes the doubt further - even the gods are later than creation, and the highest overseer 'knows not'; the two hymns frame the Vedic philosophy of origin.

secondary_sources.work: Jan Gonda, The Vision of the Vedic Poets

title.en: Indra Slays Vritra and Frees the Rivers
title.zh: 因陀羅誅弗栗多，釋放眾水

region.zh: 印度河-薩拉斯瓦蒂河平原（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 1, Hymn 32 (with 1.11, 2.11-12)

summary.en: Vritra, the coverer, coils around the waters and holds the rivers hostage in the mountain's hollow. Indra, made almighty by draughts of Soma, hurls the thunderbolt forged by Tvashtar, splits the serpent, and the pent-up rivers rush down like bellowing chariot-teams - the archetypal storm-god combat that keeps the world's waters moving and rains falling.
summary.zh: 弗栗多（『遮蔽者』）盤踞眾水，將河流挾持於山腹之內。因陀羅飲蘇摩酒而獲全能，擲由特瓦斯特利鍛造之雷霆杵，劈開巨蛇；被囚之河如怒吼的戰車群奔湧而下——此為風暴之神戰鬥的原型，使世界之水常流、雨澤常降。

sensitivity.note: Ancient liturgical-hymn source, still recited in Vedic study. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Now let me declare the heroic deeds of Indra, the first that he achieved: he slew the dragon that lay against the mountain. Tvashtar forged the bolt for him; like bellowing cows with flowing milk, the waters rushed down to the ocean. Strong of purpose, he took the Soma, drank its pressed juices, and the worshipper's gift made him mighty.

When in his hands he took the thunderbolt, the missile that slays, the lightning made of a hundred joints, he slew the first-born of dragons. Like a tree-trunk felled by the axe, the serpent lay flattened on the ground; the waters, like bellowing chariot-teams, poured over the body as they flowed away.

Vritra had grown insolent with strength; Indra, whose anger grew with the Soma he had drunk, split the serpent's head with the great bolt, and the conquered Vritra sank under his blow. The pent-up mothers of the world - the rivers - flowed on for their lord; they went, the waters, straight to the ocean, forced through the gap Indra had opened.

texts.canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda, 2nd ed., Benares, 1896 (public domain); critical: Jamison & Brereton, The Rigveda, Oxford, 2014

narrative.en:
The combat of Indra and Vritra is the epicentre of Vedic mythology - a fight retold, alluded to and re-imagined across dozens of Rigveda hymns, and the single deed by which Indra is king of the gods.

The adversary: Vritra, whose name means 'the coverer' or 'obstructor', a dragon-serpent coiled around the world's waters, gripping the rivers in the hollows of the mountains so that no rain falls and the land lies parched. The Rigveda calls him 'the first-born of dragons', the worst of Vritras; in some hymns he is a three-headed being, in others a vast serpent guarding the foot of the world-mountain, hoarding the cows of light as well as the waters.

The hero: Indra is born for this fight. The later myths tell of his miraculous birth from the side of his mother, of the thunderbolt Tvashtar the divine smith forged for him, of the hundred-jointed missile that no one else could carry. But the immediate engine of victory is Soma: Indra drinks the pressed juice of the Soma plant until his body swells with power - the hymns are candid that the god is intoxicated by the sacrifice, that the drink 'made him mighty', that his rage and his arms grow with each draught. The priests' libations are, quite literally, his ammunition: ritual and myth are one economy.

The fight: when Indra took the bolt in his hands, he slew the first-born of dragons. Vritra is not merely killed but undone - struck in the head, he collapses 'like a tree-trunk felled by the axe', and Indra leaves his vast body lying across the landscape. Then the release: the rivers, pent up like cows whose milk had been withheld, burst through the gap Indra cut and pour down to the ocean 'like bellowing chariot-teams' or 'like bellowing cows with flowing milk', washing over the dead serpent as they go. The sun rises on the freed world; dawns shine again.

Function: this is a rain-and-river myth and a liturgical charter at once. Every monsoon is a repetition of Indra's victory; every drought is Vritra's grip returning; and every Soma offering re-arms the god. The combat also maps cosmic order: Indra's bolt establishes the partition of heaven and earth, and the freed waters establish the flow of life. Comparative mythologists see here the same duel as Marduk-Tiamat (dragon of the waters), Baal-Yam (sea-serpent), and Zeus-Typhon - the storm god slaying the water-dragon to institute order.

The ambiguity: Vritra in several texts is not simply evil - some Brahmana recensions make him a Brahmin slain by Indra, and the god must perform expiation. The verse that makes Vritra 'like a Brahmin among the gods' forced later theology to negotiate: Indra's kingship is stained by the very deed that founds it, a paradox the Upanishadic and Puranic layers will inherit.
narrative.zh: 因陀羅與弗栗多之戰為吠陀神話的震央：數十首頌歌反覆重述、暗示、重構此戰，此功績奠定因陀羅之天帝之位。對手弗栗多，意為『遮蔽者』，蛇龍盤繞世界之水，將河流挾於山腹，使雨澤不降、大地乾涸；吠陀稱其為『龍之長子』、弗栗多中最惡者。英雄因陀羅為此戰而生：特瓦斯特利為其鍛造雷霆杵，百節之彌無人能舉；然勝利之引擎為蘇摩——因陀羅飲榨出的蘇摩汁直至神力充盈，頌詩坦承此神因祭酒而醉、因飲而壯，祭司的澆祭即其彈藥：儀式與神話同屬一種經濟。戰鬥：因陀羅執杵在手，誅龍之長子；弗栗多不僅被殺更被『解散』——擊首而倒，『如斧斫之樹幹』，橫陳大地。隨之釋放：被囚之河如乳汁被扣的母牛，自因陀羅所開之隙衝出，『如怒吼的戰車群』奔流入海，水漫過蛇屍。太陽於解放之世升起，黎明重輝。功能：此為雨河神話亦是禮儀憲章——每場季雨皆因陀羅之勝的重演，每場旱災皆弗栗多之掌握復歸，每次蘇摩祭皆為神再武裝。比較神話學視之與馬爾杜克-提亞馬特、巴力-雅姆、宙斯-提豐同型：風暴神誅水龍以立秩序。曖昧處：若干梵書使弗栗多為婆羅門，因陀羅因而負殺婆羅門之罪，須行贖罪——因陀羅之王權正因其奠基之功而蒙污，此悖論為奧義書與往世書層所承繼。

functions: Aition of rain, rivers and the monsoon - the storm god keeps the waters moving
Liturgical charter of Soma sacrifice (the god's power purchased with libations)
Archetype of the storm-god vs. water-dragon combat across the ancient Near East and Indo-European world
Origin of Indra's kingship - and of the brahminicide-guilt paradox later theology must expiate

variants.name: Ugaritic Baal-Yam combat

title.en: Yama and Yami: The First Mortal and the Forbidden Twin
title.zh: 閻摩與閻蜜：第一位死者和被禁的雙生姊妹

region.en: Yama's realm (symbolic pin at Gaya, city of ancestor rites)
region.zh: 閻摩之國（象徵性定位於伽耶，祖先祭祀之城）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10 (late mandala), c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 10 (Yama-Yami dialogue; with 10.14 Yama's funeral hymn)

summary.en: Yama, the first mortal to die, finds the road to the pastures of the dead and becomes their king. His twin sister Yami presses him to beget the race with her - 'the makers of mankind made us man and wife in the womb'; Yama refuses: the gods watch the holy law, and no later age will accept what the first age did. The dialogue fixes two foundations at once: death's realm and the incest taboo.
summary.zh: 閻摩為第一位死去之人，尋得通往亡者牧場之路，遂為其王。其雙生姊妹閻蜜懇求與之交合以繁衍族類——『造人者在胎中已以夫妻相成』；閻摩拒絕：諸神守望聖法，後世必不容太初所為。此對話同時奠定兩事：死亡之國與亂倫之禁。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Yama worship and ancestor rites (sraddha) continue. Classified 'myth'. The origin-of-death tagging is interpretive (Thompson index is Euro-American) - noted here.

passages.text: Yami speaks to her twin, urgent as a lover: she calls him her husband in the sight of the gods who made them one being in the womb. Even the maker, she says, formed us man and wife; the whole race of gods and mortals comes from such unions - why should Yama alone be restrained? Come to me, my brother; throw your arms about me.

Yama answers with the law: the gods watch with vigilance over their holy ordinances; the speech he speaks does not fit her. The eyes of all beings are upon them; the deeds of the primal ages will not be repeated - later ages will not let what the first ones did stand for them. He cites Tvashtri the maker, who created the pair with separate purposes, and tells her plainly: seek another husband and make him thy partner; join with him and be a mother. Yami retorts that a brother's harshness is pitiable; Yama closes: another husband is found for her - with Yama she shall never lie.

Elsewhere the hymns tell what became of Yama: he chose death and found the path for the many; he was the first to reach the pasture where the ancient herdsmen and their flocks have gone, the first to mark out the meeting-place of the dead. In the house of the fathers his seat is established; he gathers the mortals of old around him, king of the dead, and men still offer to him as they send their fathers ahead by fire.

texts.canonical_translation: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda, 2nd ed., Benares, 1896 (public domain); critical: Jamison & Brereton, The Rigveda, Oxford, 2014

narrative.en:
Book 10 of the Rigveda contains the tradition's earliest speculation on where death came from, and it does so twice over: in a dialogue about incest, and in funeral hymns about a first traveler. The Yama-Yami dialogue (10.10) is the archetypal origin-of-death-and-kinship-law myth of the Indo-European world.

The situation: Yama and Yami are twins, the first humans born to the creator. Yama, in the Vedic frame, is mortal - the first man to die, the one who chose death and thereby discovered the path to the world of the fathers, where he reigns as king of the pastures where the dead graze like an ancient herd. Yami, his twin, remains alive and unmarried. She speaks first, and her logic is radical: there is no one else. If humanity is to continue, the pair must pair. She reminds him that even the creator formed them 'man and wife in the womb', and that gods and mortals descend from such unions; the first generation cannot be bound by the customs of later ones.

Yama's refusal is the founding argument of the taboo. He invokes surveillance: 'the gods watch with vigilance over their holy law' - the transgression would be seen. He distinguishes epochs: what the first age did, no later age will accept - the taboo is historical, a rule about what may be done 'now that there are later ages'. He appeals to the maker's intent: Tvashtri formed the pair with distinct purposes, not as one flesh. And he offers an exit: another husband exists for her; let her join with him and be a mother. Yami's reply is bitter - she calls his harshness pitiable - and Yama's closing line is absolute: with Yama she shall never lie.

The two halves fit together. The funeral hymns (10.14 and the Yama hymns of Book 10) show Yama as the first to die and the pathfinder of death - he goes first, so that the dead have somewhere to go and a king who receives them. The dialogue with Yami explains why there are no more primeval unions: the first twins did not become the parents of humanity; the race descends instead through ordinary marriage, bounded by the law Yama defended. Death is Yama's own story: to be mortal is to be the species of Yama, who went ahead.

Comparatively, this is the same constellation as the sibling-creator pairs of many cosmogonies - but with a refusal where others have union. The taboo turned into doctrine: Yama's realm (Yamaloka) becomes the intermediate station of the dead in the epics and Puranas, and the Katha Upanishad makes him the teacher who can promise immortality but insists on the law (dharma) as the way.

Function: the dialogue legitimizes exogamy and the incest taboo as divine law with a memory of a first exception; the funeral hymns make Yama the friendly face of necessity - the first traveler who keeps records, receives offerings, and in folk practice is still fed at ancestor rites.
narrative.zh: 梨俱吠陀第十卷含此傳統最早對死亡來源的思辨，分兩次呈現：一場關於亂倫的對話，與數首關於第一位旅人的葬歌。閻摩與閻蜜為雙生，創造者所生之首批人類。吠陀框架中閻摩為有死者——第一位選擇死亡之人，因而發現通往亡者世界之路，在亡者如古牧群般放牧的牧野為王。閻蜜仍活而未嫁，她先開口，邏輯極端：世上再無他人；族類若要延續，雙生必須成偶。她提醒他：連造物者也在胎中以夫妻相成；諸神與凡人皆出自此類結合；太初世代不受後世風俗束縛。閻摩之拒絕是禁忌的立論基礎：他訴諸監視——『諸神以警醒守望其聖法』；訴諸時代——太初所為，後世不容；訴諸造者之意——特瓦斯特利以不同目的造此一對，非使其為一體；並給出出口——另有夫婿存在，可與之成婚為母。閻蜜之答苦澀，斥其嚴苛可憫；閻摩結語絕對：與閻摩同寢，永不。兩半相合：葬歌顯示閻摩為第一位死者、死亡之路的開闢者——他先行，故亡者有可去之處、有收留之王；對話則解釋為何再無太初結合：首對雙生未成人類之父母，族類遂經由閻摩所守之法律界定的平常婚姻而繁衍。功能：對話使外婚制與亂倫禁忌合法化為帶有太初例外記憶的神聖法律；葬歌使閻摩成為必然性之親切面孔——先行旅人、記錄分毫不差、接受祭品，至今仍在祖先祭祀中受饗。

variants.name: Shatapatha Brahmana's Yama-Yami
variants.summary: Yama and Yami are fully paired there - the union is accepted as the act by which the human race begins, the taboo softened into ritual genealogy; the two tellings bracket the tradition's ambivalence.

variants.name: Katha Upanishad's Yama as teacher
variants.summary: The king of the dead becomes the guru who teaches Nachiketas that the Self is unborn; death's king is turned into the revealer of what death is not.

variants.name: Puranic Yama (Chitragupta's ledgers)
variants.text_tradition: Purana corpus (e.g. Agni, Garuda Purana), c. 4th-10th c. CE
variants.summary: Yama's realm becomes a bureaucracy: Chitragupta records deeds, Yamadutas drag the dead, and the first traveler is now a judge with assessors - the pastoral king recast as accountant.
